nameStory: The Black-headed Gull gets its name from the dark chocolate-brown hood it wears during breeding season, though it's not truly black. The scientific name tells a fun story too - 'ridibundus' is Latin for 'laughing,' referring to their chattering, almost giggling call that sounds like they're sharing jokes with their flock mates.
description: The Black-headed Gull is a small, elegant seabird that's about the size of a crow with long, pointed wings built for graceful flight. During breeding season, adults sport a distinctive dark brown 'hood' covering their head, while in winter this fades to just a dark spot behind the eye. They have bright red legs and bill, white bodies, and pale gray wings with black wingtips. These European visitors are uncommon but regular guests to New England's coasts.

idTips.label: Seasonal head pattern
idTips.description: In spring and summer, look for the distinctive dark chocolate-brown hood that covers the entire head except around the eyes; in fall and winter, this becomes just a dark ear spot and smudgy cap

idTips.label: Bill and leg color
idTips.description: Bright red-orange bill and legs that stand out like little orange markers against their white body - much more vivid than the duller pink of most other small gulls

idTips.label: Wing pattern in flight
idTips.description: Watch for distinctive white leading edge along the front of dark-tipped wings, creating a bright white 'headlight' effect that flashes as they fly

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more delicate than Ring-billed or Herring Gulls, with a more tern-like graceful flight style and thinner, more pointed wings

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Listen for their distinctive laughing chatter - a series of harsh 'kek-kek-kek' calls that sound almost like they're cackling at a private joke

habitat: Look for Black-headed Gulls along New England's coastline, particularly at beaches, harbors, and estuaries where they mix with flocks of other gulls. They're often found at mudflats, tidal pools, and around fishing piers where they can pick up small fish and invertebrates. Occasionally spotted at large inland lakes and reservoirs, especially during migration periods.

seasonality.spring: Arriving migrants may show the beginnings of their dark hood development, with patchy brown coloring appearing on the head. Peak time to spot them as they pass through on their way north.
seasonality.summer: Rare but possible visitors showing full breeding plumage with complete dark brown hood and bright red bill and legs. Most striking and easiest to identify during this season.
seasonality.fall: More commonly observed during fall migration when their hood is molting away, leaving distinctive dark ear spots and partial caps that can help with identification.
seasonality.winter: Occasional visitors in basic plumage with white heads marked only by dark ear spots and smudgy caps, requiring careful attention to bill color and wing patterns for proper identification.

funFact: Black-headed Gulls are one of the few gull species that regularly steal food by following plows in farmer's fields, walking directly behind tractors like feathered farm hands to snatch up earthworms and insects turned up by the machinery.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Bonaparte's Gull, but Black-headed Gulls are slightly larger with red (not black) bills, red (not pink) legs, and darker wingtip patterns. Memory trick: 'Red legs and bill = real Black-headed Gull' (even though Bonaparte's also gets a dark hood).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'black-headed,' the hood is actually dark chocolate brown, not true black. These are primarily European birds that occasionally wander to North America, making any sighting in New England a special treat for birders.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Bonaparte's Gull, the Black-headed Gull is slightly larger and stockier with a more robust build. The key differences are the bright red-orange bill and legs (versus Bonaparte's black bill and pink legs) and the slightly different wing pattern with more extensive black on the wingtips. Both species get dark heads in breeding season, but the Black-headed Gull's hood extends further and appears more solidly colored.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bonaparte's Gull is much smaller and more delicate than its closest New England relative, the Black-headed Gull.
